title: Copy-scarce learning of ground states
abstract: Probing multiple properties of ground states is central to understanding quantum matter, yet conventional readout can be prohibitively costly because it consumes many independently prepared copies. Here, in copy-scarce regimes, we establish optimal trade-offs between the number of initial ground-state copies and elapsed Hamiltonian-evolution time required for estimating multiple observables or reconstructing a full classical description of a unique gapped ground state. We derive a unifying inequality that quantifies how well ground states can be distinguished using initial copies and controlled dynamics, even when all copies may be consumed. It yields worst-case lower bounds on elapsed Hamiltonian time that any protocol must incur to perform either task. We construct parallel catalytic readouts that return all initial copies nearly unchanged while attaining these bounds up to poly-logarithmic factors. Our protocols require no coherent preparation circuit or its inverse, and their elapsed Hamiltonian time depends only logarithmically on the inverse of the desired return error. Thus, optimal copy--dynamics trade-offs can be attained together with catalytic return. Numerical benchmarks further show substantial reductions in end-to-end elapsed Hamiltonian time relative to a task-specialized copy-consuming protocol, even under an optimistic preparation-cost model. Our results reveal a copy--dynamics resource landscape connecting copy-scarce learning to copy-only endpoints realized by known protocols for shadow tomography and pure-state tomography.
summary: This work establishes optimal resource trade-offs for estimating multiple ground-state observables in copy-scarce regimes. By developing catalytic readout protocols, the authors achieve near-optimal measurement accuracy while crucially returning the initial quantum copies nearly unchanged. This advances the understanding of quantum resource management in quantum sensing and characterization.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of estimating multiple ground-state observables when conventional readout methods are too costly due to the need for many independent copies.
main_result: They derive a unifying inequality and construct catalytic readout protocols that achieve near-optimal trade-offs between initial copies and evolution time while returning the initial copies nearly unchanged.
method: The approach involves deriving lower bounds via a static–dynamic distinguishability inequality and constructing parallel catalytic readout protocols utilizing controlled Hamiltonian evolution.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on a quantum system with a unique, gapped ground state $|\psi_0angle$ governed by a Hamiltonian $H$. The task is estimating expectation values $\mu_j = \langle\psi_0|O_j|\psi_0angle$ for multiple observables $O_j$.
key_observables: Expectation values of multiple observables ($\mu_j$), the number of initial copies ($P$), and the elapsed Hamiltonian time ($T$).
important_parameters: The spectral gap ($\Delta$) of the Hamiltonian, the desired error ($\epsilon$), and the number of observables ($M$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a unique gapped ground state and controlled access to Hamiltonian evolution $e^{-itH}$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the optimal copy–dynamics trade-off with catalytic return, showing the general measurement circuit and the return of copies. Figure 2 details the readout process, including the joint phase-kickback mechanism for multi-signal extension.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the core problem, derives the fundamental lower bound inequality, constructs the catalytic readout protocols achieving the bound, and concludes with numerical benchmarks comparing the new method to specialized, copy-consuming protocols.
why_interesting: The focus on resource trade-offs (copies vs. time) and the development of catalytic protocols that preserve quantum resources are highly relevant to quantum computation and quantum metrology.
